y0: He put a child in the middle
y1: Jesus had predicted His suffering twice, but the disciples were asking, 'Who is the greatest?' Jesus puts a child 'in the middle'. At that time, children had neither legal rights nor status.
y2: “Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” Then He gives a severe warning to those who cause the little ones to stumble: it would be better for them to have a millstone hung around their neck and be thrown into the sea.
y3: “Unless you change and become like little children.” Even those who are already disciples need to 'change'. The main characteristic of a child is 'dependence' rather than innocence. It is knowing you cannot stand on your own and leaning on the Father.
y5: While the lost sheep in Luke 15 is about a 'lost sinner', the lost sheep in Matthew 18 is about a little one who has 'gone astray' within the church. It refers to a weak brother or sister in the community.
y6: “Your Father in heaven does not want any of these little ones to perish.” By the numbers, 99% remain, but for God, the 'one' is everything.
y7: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18:10). The little ones are by no means small before God. Like courtiers who constantly see the king's face in the palace, their situation is immediately reported to God.
y8: The way to win over your brother
y9: If a brother sins, you should first speak to him one-on-one, then with one or two others, and then tell it to the church. The goal is not punishment, but to 'win over your brother'. This is the way to seek the lost sheep.
y10: Peter asked, “Should I forgive up to seven times?” Rabbis said three times was enough, so Peter was speaking generously. Jesus says, “Not seven times, but seventy-seven times.” This means do not keep count.
y11: In Genesis 4:24, Lamech boasted of his revenge, saying, “If Cain is avenged seven times, then Lamech seventy-seven times.” Jesus takes that number and reverses it into a number of forgiveness.
y12: Ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii
y13: The servant's debt was ten thousand talents. Since one talent was about 15–20 years' wages for a laborer, ten thousand talents was an amount he could not pay even if he worked a thousand lifetimes. His fellow servant's debt to him was a hundred denarii, about three months' wages.
y14: The king had mercy and forgave it all, but he grabbed his fellow servant by the throat. “Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?” Only a person who knows the greatness of the forgiveness they received from God can forgive someone else.
y15: “Unless you forgive your brother from your heart.” Forgiveness starts with a decision, not a feeling. Even if the wound doesn't heal immediately, it is the decision to tear up the debt paper before God. Forgiving does not mean saying the wrong was 'okay'.
verse: “Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.””
prayer: Our Father in heaven, thank You for not wanting anyone to perish and for coming to look for me when I went astray. Instead of arguing about 'who is the greatest', let me be someone who places the little ones in the center. Remembering the ten thousand talent forgiveness I received, help me to forgive my brother from my heart. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: humble. This is the same humility Jesus speaks of when He says, 'I am gentle and humble in heart' (Matthew 11:29). “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12).
d1: forgive. This is the same verb as 'forgive us our debts' in the Lord's Prayer. It means letting go of what you are holding onto. Read together with Matthew 6:12 and 6:14–15.
d2: talent. About 6,000 denarii, roughly 20 years' wages for a laborer. 'Ten thousand' (myrioi) is the largest numerical unit in Greek. It means unpayable. The same unit appears in the parable of the talents in chapter 25.
